purpose: Tetracaine is a numbing medicine used to temporarily block pain in a specific area of your body. It is commonly used in the eyes before eye exams or procedures, and sometimes on the skin or mucous membranes before minor medical procedures. It helps your doctor or nurse work more comfortably without causing you pain.
how_it_works: Tetracaine works by temporarily blocking the nerve signals in the area where it is applied. Think of it like putting a pause button on the nerves so they cannot send pain messages to your brain. Once the medicine wears off, feeling returns to normal on its own.
common_side_effects: In the eye, you may feel a brief stinging or burning sensation right when the drops are put in. Your eye may look a little red for a short time. On the skin, you might notice mild irritation, redness, or a temporary tingling feeling where it was applied.
warnings: Do not rub your eye after eye drops are used, since you won't feel pain and could accidentally hurt your eye. Tetracaine should only be used by a healthcare provider — it is not meant for you to use at home on your own, especially in the eyes. Tell your doctor or pharmacist if you have any allergies to numbing medicines, and let them know all the medicines you are taking. Using too much can cause serious problems with your heart or nervous system.
typical_dosing: For eye procedures, a healthcare provider will usually place 1 to 2 drops in the affected eye. For skin or mucous membrane use, a small amount of gel or solution is applied directly to the area. The dose and how often it is used depends entirely on the procedure and your provider's instructions — you should never apply it yourself at home unless specifically told to do so.
